title: Processes & Threads
tagline: How your OS juggles millions of tasks at once

sections.content:
Every program you run becomes a **process** — an isolated unit with its own memory, file handles, and CPU registers. Processes are the OS's fundamental unit of isolation: if one crashes, the others survive. But spawning a new process is expensive, so modern programs use **threads** — lightweight execution units that share the same address space within a process.

Understanding processes and threads unlocks how your code actually runs on hardware, why `setTimeout` behaves the way it does in Node.js, and why shared mutable state is so dangerous in concurrent systems.

sections.mermaid:
stateDiagram-v2
  [*] --> New : fork() / exec()
  New --> Ready : admitted to run queue
  Ready --> Running : scheduler dispatches
  Running --> Ready : time slice expires
  Running --> Waiting : I/O or event wait
  Waiting --> Ready : I/O complete
  Running --> Terminated : exit() called
  Terminated --> [*]
sections.caption: Process lifecycle: a process moves through New → Ready → Running → Waiting and back, until it terminates.

sections.title: Restaurant Kitchen Analogy
sections.content:
Think of a **process** as an entire restaurant: it has its own building (address space), kitchen equipment (resources), and staff (threads). Two restaurants don't share ovens — isolation is guaranteed.

A **thread** is one cook inside that kitchen. Multiple cooks share the same ovens, refrigerators, and prep tables (heap memory, file handles). They can collaborate quickly, but if one cook knocks over the mise-en-place, every cook is affected. A **context switch** between threads is like one cook stepping back and another stepping up to the same station — fast, but requires saving where the first cook left off (register state).

sections.title: Process vs Thread: What Actually Differs
sections.content:
A process owns a complete **address space**: code segment, stack, heap, and BSS. When the OS forks a process, it copies (or copy-on-writes) all of that memory — expensive. A thread, by contrast, gets only its own **stack and register file**; everything else is shared with sibling threads in the same process.

**Context switching** is the mechanism by which the CPU stops one task and resumes another. For processes, the OS must flush the TLB (translation lookaside buffer) and swap memory maps. For threads within the same process, the address space stays the same — only registers and the stack pointer change, making thread switches ~10× cheaper than process switches.

**Concurrency** means multiple tasks *appear* to progress simultaneously (even on one core, via rapid switching). **Parallelism** means tasks *actually* run at the same instant on multiple CPU cores. JavaScript's event loop is concurrent but single-threaded — no true parallelism on the main thread. Worker threads in Node.js enable actual parallelism.

sections.label: Runtime
sections.explanation: Node.js `worker_threads` creates OS-level threads sharing the same process. Each worker gets its own V8 isolate (stack + heap snapshot), but they can share `SharedArrayBuffer` memory — illustrating the thread model. CPU-bound tasks run truly in parallel without blocking the event loop.

sections.label: Concept

sections.content: **Rule of thumb for thread count:** CPU-bound tasks → threads ≈ number of CPU cores (`navigator.hardwareConcurrency` in browsers, `os.cpus().length` in Node.js). I/O-bound tasks → more threads are fine because they spend most time waiting, not computing.

items: A **process** is an isolated program instance with its own address space; a **thread** is a lightweight execution unit that shares the process's memory.
**Context switching** saves and restores CPU register state; thread switches are cheaper than process switches because the address space doesn't change.
**Concurrency** is about managing multiple tasks at once (even on one core); **parallelism** is about executing tasks simultaneously on multiple cores.
Process states follow the lifecycle: New → Ready → Running → Waiting → Terminated — driven by the OS scheduler.
Node.js is single-threaded by default (concurrent, not parallel); `worker_threads` enables true CPU parallelism within one process.

quiz.question: What does a thread share with other threads in the same process?
options: Its own private stack and heap
The process's heap, code segment, and file handles
quiz.explanation: Threads within the same process share the heap, code segment, and open file handles. Each thread only owns its own stack and CPU register snapshot.

quiz.question: Which process state comes immediately after a process is admitted to the run queue?
quiz.explanation: After being admitted from 'New', a process enters the 'Ready' state. It stays there until the scheduler dispatches it to the CPU, at which point it moves to 'Running'.

quiz.question: Why is a thread context switch faster than a process context switch?
options: The OS doesn't need to flush the TLB or swap address spaces
Threads never need to save register state
The CPU runs threads at a higher clock speed
quiz.explanation: When switching between threads in the same process, the virtual address space remains the same — no TLB flush or memory map swap is needed. Only registers and the stack pointer must be saved/restored.

quiz.question: What is the difference between concurrency and parallelism?
options: Concurrency requires multiple CPU cores; parallelism does not
Parallelism means tasks appear to run simultaneously; concurrency means they actually do
Concurrency means multiple tasks make progress (possibly on one core); parallelism means tasks run at the same instant on multiple cores
quiz.explanation: Concurrency is about structure — multiple tasks can make progress, possibly interleaved on one core. Parallelism is about execution — tasks run at exactly the same time on different cores.

quiz.question: A Node.js program uses `Promise.all([fetchA(), fetchB()])`. This is an example of:
quiz.explanation: Node.js has a single-threaded event loop. `Promise.all` interleaves async tasks concurrently — both can be 'in flight' at once — but they run on one thread, not in parallel.

quiz.question: A process moves from Running to Waiting. What most likely caused this?
options: It requested I/O or is waiting for an event
quiz.explanation: A process transitions to Waiting when it blocks on I/O (disk read, network call) or waits for a synchronization event. It returns to Ready once the I/O completes.

quiz.question: Linux's Completely Fair Scheduler (CFS) picks the next process to run based on:
quiz.explanation: CFS tracks each task's virtual runtime — how long it has run weighted by priority. It always picks the task with the smallest vruntime next, ensuring fairness across all processes.

quiz.question: How many worker threads is generally optimal for CPU-bound tasks?
options: Approximately equal to the number of CPU cores
As many as possible to maximize throughput
quiz.explanation: For CPU-bound work, having more threads than cores causes context-switch overhead with no throughput gain. Matching thread count to core count keeps all cores busy without unnecessary switching.

quiz.question: What happens to a process's address space when the OS performs a fork()?
options: The child immediately gets a fully separate physical copy of all memory
The address space is shared using copy-on-write until either process writes
The child has no memory until it calls exec()
The parent's memory is destroyed and transferred to the child
quiz.explanation: Modern OSes use copy-on-write (CoW): the parent and child initially share the same physical pages. A private copy is only made for a page when one of the processes writes to it, saving memory and time.

quiz.question: Which resource does each thread exclusively own (not shared with sibling threads)?
quiz.explanation: Each thread owns its own call stack (local variables, return addresses) and a snapshot of CPU registers (program counter, stack pointer, general-purpose registers). All other resources are shared among threads in the same process.
